questions.stem: A 44 year old man has a 4 month history of tiredness, weight loss of 6 kg and vague abdominal pain. He feels lightheaded when he stands up and has started adding salt to all his food. His skin looks tanned although he has not been abroad. His BP is 102/64 mmHg lying and 84/52 mmHg standing.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fatigue, weight loss, salt craving, postural hypotension, pigmentation, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and low glucose are primary adrenal insufficiency.

clues: adding salt to all his food
steps.x: Salt craving, pigmentation and a postural drop with low sodium and high potassium.

elim: Causes weight loss and abdominal pain but not hyperkalaemia, postural hypotension or pigmentation.
Causes weight gain and cold intolerance.
Weight loss and pain, but not salt craving, hyperkalaemia or pigmentation.
Causes euvolaemic hyponatraemia with a normal potassium and no hypotension.

steps.x: A: Addison's disease. Pigmented, salt-craving, hypotensive with Na down and K up = Addison's.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has a 3 month history of fatigue, nausea and dizziness on standing. Her 9am cortisol is low. Her GP is not sure whether the problem is in the adrenal glands themselves or in the pituitary gland.
questions.q: Which clinical finding would best support primary rather than secondary adrenal insufficiency?
questions.e: Hyperpigmentation from high ACTH occurs in primary but not secondary adrenal insufficiency; it is the key distinguishing feature.

clues: adrenal glands themselves or in the pituitary gland
steps.x: Only primary disease has a high ACTH.

elim: Occurs in both primary and secondary disease.
Cortisol deficiency causes it in both.
Low in both primary and secondary disease.
Occurs in both.

steps.x: B: Hyperpigmentation of the skin creases. Pigmentation = high ACTH = primary adrenal insufficiency.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man who moved from India 10 years ago has a 6 month history of fatigue, weight loss and dizziness on standing. He was treated for pulmonary tuberculosis as a young man. A short Synacthen test confirms primary adrenal insufficiency. Adrenal autoantibodies are negative and CT shows calcified adrenal glands.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause?
questions.e: TB adrenalitis is a cause of Addison's disease, classically with adrenal calcification; autoimmune adrenalitis is the commonest cause in the UK.

steps.x: Previous TB, negative antibodies and calcified adrenals.

elim: Usually soft tissue masses in a patient with a known cancer, not calcified glands.
The commonest cause overall, but autoantibodies are negative and autoimmune glands are small, not calcified.
Acute, in meningococcal septicaemia or anticoagulation.
He takes no steroids and this causes secondary insufficiency.

steps.x: E: Tuberculous adrenalitis. Calcified adrenals + previous TB = TB adrenalitis.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with severe asthma has used high-dose inhaled fluticasone for years and has had six courses of oral prednisolone in the past year. She stopped all her inhalers a month ago because she felt well. She now has fatigue, nausea and dizziness on standing. Her 9am cortisol is low.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her adrenal insufficiency?
questions.e: Exogenous steroids, even regular inhaled steroids, suppress the axis; stopping them suddenly causes adrenal insufficiency.

steps.x: Long-term steroids stopped suddenly.

elim: No cancer history; unusual at her age.
The commonest cause overall, but the steroid history explains this.
Presents in infancy or with virilisation.
No TB history or risk factors.

steps.x: D: Exogenous steroid use. Iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency from steroids, including inhaled ones.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man with advanced HIV has a CD4 count of 30 cells/mm3 and is not taking antiretrovirals. He has a 2 month history of tiredness, weight loss and dizziness on standing. His sodium is 128 mmol/L and potassium 5.7 mmol/L. A short Synacthen test shows an inadequate cortisol response.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his adrenal insufficiency?
o: Opportunistic infection of the adrenal glands
questions.e: Fungal and opportunistic infections in HIV (for example CMV) can destroy the adrenal cortex and cause Addison's disease.

steps.x: Primary adrenal insufficiency (high potassium) in severe immunosuppression.

elim: Possible, but in advanced HIV infections such as CMV are a recognised cause.
He is not taking steroids.
Would cause secondary insufficiency without hyperkalaemia.
Acute haemorrhage in meningococcal sepsis, not 2 months of symptoms.

steps.x: C: Opportunistic infection of the adrenal glands. Advanced HIV: opportunistic adrenalitis.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman with type 1 diabetes and vitiligo has had three hypoglycaemic episodes in a month and has needed to cut her insulin doses. She feels tired, nauseated and dizzy on standing, and her skin creases look darker. Her HbA1c has fallen from 62 to 49 mmol/mol.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Addison's disease is associated with other autoimmune conditions (type 1 diabetes, vitiligo, thyroid disease); cortisol deficiency increases insulin sensitivity, causing hypoglycaemia.

steps.x: Autoimmune background, falling insulin needs, pigmentation and postural symptoms.

elim: Can cause hypoglycaemia in type 1 diabetes but not darker creases or postural dizziness.
Causes erratic glucose and vomiting, but not pigmentation.
Causes weight gain and cold intolerance, not pigmentation.
Causes hypoglycaemia in people without diabetes; no pigmentation.

steps.x: A: Addison's disease. T1DM with new hypos and pigmentation: think Addison's.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman takes prednisolone 15 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica. She was kept nil by mouth for 2 days after an emergency hernia repair and her steroids were not given. She is now drowsy and hypotensive despite 2 L of IV fluid. Her temperature is 36.4°C, BP 74/40 mmHg and pulse rate 122 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Missed steroids in a long-term user plus the stress of surgery precipitate an adrenal crisis: shock refractory to fluids, hypoglycaemia, hyperkalaemia and mild hyponatraemia.

clues: hypotensive despite 2 L of IV fluid
steps.x: Long-term steroids missed during surgical stress, with shock and hypoglycaemia.

elim: Hernia repair has no anastomosis; would cause peritonitis.
Haemoglobin is normal and there is no bleeding.
Would cause hypoxia and does not explain hypoglycaemia or hyperkalaemia.
No fever or source; hypoglycaemia and hyperkalaemia point to steroid deficiency.

steps.x: A: Adrenal crisis. Steroid user + stress + missed doses + shock = adrenal crisis.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has a 5 month history of fatigue, weight loss and dizziness on standing. A short Synacthen test confirms primary adrenal insufficiency. She mentions a change in her body that has worried her.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
o: Thinning of axillary and pubic hair
questions.e: In women with Addison's disease, loss of adrenal androgens causes thinning of pubic and axillary hair; palmar creases are pigmented.

steps.x: In women the adrenal cortex is the main androgen source.

elim: Features of Cushing's syndrome (cortisol excess).
Suggests thyroid disease.
Suggests androgen excess, the opposite problem.
She would have dark, not pale, creases.

steps.x: E: Thinning of axillary and pubic hair. Women with Addison's lose axillary and pubic hair.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has a 3 month history of tiredness, lightheadedness when standing and weight loss. His sodium is 129 mmol/L and potassium 5.6 mmol/L. His skin creases are darker than before. The GP asks about his diet.
questions.q: Which symptom is he most likely to report?
questions.e: Aldosterone deficiency causes salt loss, so patients with Addison's disease often crave salty food.

steps.x: Salt-wasting primary adrenal insufficiency.

elim: Pica, a feature of iron deficiency.
A feature of hyperthyroidism.
He is losing weight with a poor appetite.
Suggest diabetes mellitus or hypercalcaemia.

steps.x: B: Craving salty food. Addison's: salt craving.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has newly diagnosed autoimmune Addison's disease. Her sodium is 126 mmol/L and potassium 6.1 mmol/L. Her consultant explains that the different layers of the adrenal cortex make different hormones.
questions.q: Loss of which hormone is the most likely cause of her hyperkalaemia?
o: Adrenal androgens from the zona reticularis
Antidiuretic hormone from the posterior pituitary
questions.e: The zona glomerulosa makes aldosterone, which controls sodium and potassium balance; the zona fasciculata makes cortisol.

clues: different layers of the adrenal cortex
steps.x: Potassium excretion depends on a mineralocorticoid.

elim: Do not control potassium.
The medulla is spared and adrenaline does not drive potassium excretion.
Not an adrenal hormone; affects water, not potassium.
Cortisol deficiency causes hypoglycaemia and hypotension, not the hyperkalaemia.

steps.x: C: Aldosterone from the zona glomerulosa. Hyperkalaemia in Addison's = loss of aldosterone (zona glomerulosa).

questions.stem: A 24 year old man with Addison's disease is brought to the emergency department after 2 days of vomiting with norovirus. He could not keep his tablets down. He is confused and clammy. His BP is 70/38 mmHg and pulse rate 128 bpm. Bloods are sent.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the initial blood tests?
questions.e: Adrenal crisis: shock, hypotension, abdominal pain, common hypoglycaemia, hyperkalaemia and mild hyponatraemia.

clues: could not keep his tablets down
steps.x: Crisis after missed tablets; confusion and clamminess point to a low glucose.

elim: Hypercalcaemia, not hypocalcaemia, can occur in adrenal crisis.
Potassium is high in adrenal crisis.
Sodium is low, not high.
Adrenal crisis does not cause alkalosis; a mild acidosis is more likely.

steps.x: B: Glucose 2.4 mmol/L. Hypoglycaemia is common in adrenal crisis.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with non-small cell lung cancer has a 6 week history of fatigue, vomiting and dizziness on standing. His sodium is 127 mmol/L, potassium 5.9 mmol/L and glucose 3.8 mmol/L. His skin creases look darker. A short Synacthen test shows an inadequate response. CT shows bilateral adrenal masses.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his adrenal insufficiency?
questions.e: Malignancy, including bilateral adrenal metastases (common from lung cancer), is a cause of primary adrenal insufficiency.

steps.x: Primary adrenal insufficiency with bilateral adrenal masses in a patient with lung cancer.

elim: Gives small atrophic glands, not bilateral masses.
Causes cortisol excess with hypokalaemia.
Causes hyponatraemia with a normal potassium and normal Synacthen test.
No TB history; usually calcified glands.

steps.x: A: Adrenal metastases. Lung cancer + bilateral adrenal masses + Addison's = metastases.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has a 2 month history of tiredness and dizziness on standing. Her 9am serum cortisol is 290 nmol/L. Her sodium is 134 mmol/L and potassium 5.1 mmol/L.

visual.title: 9am serum cortisol
visual.label: 290 nmol/L
visual.caption: Between 100 and 500 nmol/L the result is inconclusive.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of the cortisol result?
o: Inconclusive; a short Synacthen test is needed
questions.e: A 9am cortisol of 100 to 500 nmol/L is inconclusive and needs a short Synacthen test, the confirmatory test.

steps.x: The value falls in the grey zone between 100 and 500.

elim: Only a low level suggests insufficiency and confirmation needs a Synacthen test.
A level of 100 to 500 nmol/L neither confirms nor excludes it.
This is not a raised cortisol.
Cortisol alone cannot locate the cause.

steps.x: C: Inconclusive; a short Synacthen test is needed. 9am cortisol 100 to 500 = do a short Synacthen test.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man has a 3 month history of fatigue, weight loss and salt craving. His GP took a serum cortisol at a 4pm appointment, which was 180 nmol/L. His sodium is 131 mmol/L and potassium 5.4 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Cortisol is lowest in the afternoon, so the initial test is a 9am serum cortisol timed to the diurnal peak.

steps.x: An afternoon cortisol is uninterpretable because of the diurnal rhythm.

elim: A test for Cushing's syndrome (cortisol excess).
A test for Cushing's syndrome.
A test for Cushing's syndrome.
Do not assess adrenal insufficiency.

steps.x: B: 9am serum cortisol. Suspected Addison's: 9am cortisol first.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman with suspected Addison's disease has a short Synacthen test. Her baseline cortisol is 180 nmol/L and her cortisol 30 minutes after IM tetracosactide is 340 nmol/L.

visual.title: 30-minute cortisol after Synacthen
visual.label: 340 nmol/L
visual.caption: An adequate response needs at least 450 nmol/L at 30 minutes.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation?
o: Inadequate response, consistent with adrenal insufficiency
questions.e: In the short Synacthen test an adequate response needs a 30-minute cortisol of 450 nmol/L or more; a smaller rise confirms adrenal insufficiency.

clues: 30 minutes after IM tetracosactide is 340 nmol/L
steps.x: 340 is below the 450 nmol/L target.

elim: An adequate response needs a 30-minute cortisol of at least 450 nmol/L.
Cortisol is low, not high.
The Synacthen test is the confirmatory test; it does not need a 9am cortisol after it.
This test assesses the adrenal response to ACTH.

steps.x: C: Inadequate response, consistent with adrenal insufficiency. Synacthen: 30-minute cortisol under 450 = adrenal insufficiency.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has a failed short Synacthen test. He has no skin pigmentation and his potassium is normal. He had a pituitary adenoma removed 2 years ago. The endocrinologist wants to know whether the adrenal insufficiency is primary, secondary or tertiary.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: A prolonged ACTH stimulation test differentiates primary, secondary and tertiary adrenal insufficiency.

steps.x: Insufficiency confirmed, but the level of the problem is unclear.

elim: Used to look for cortisol excess.
Shows adrenal structure, not where in the axis the failure lies.
Used for Cushing's syndrome.
Will give the same result and cannot locate the level.

steps.x: D: Prolonged ACTH stimulation test. To separate primary from secondary or tertiary: prolonged ACTH stimulation test.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with Hashimoto's thyroiditis has primary adrenal insufficiency confirmed on a short Synacthen test. She has no history of tuberculosis, cancer or steroid use. Her endocrinologist wants to confirm the cause.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: HIV test as the only test
questions.e: Autoimmune adrenalitis causes 80 to 90% of cases; adrenal autoantibodies (and adrenal imaging if needed) identify the cause.

clues: no history of tuberculosis, cancer or steroid use
steps.x: Another autoimmune disease and no other cause.

elim: Looks for TB, which is unlikely here.
No risk factors; autoimmune disease is far more likely.
A test for phaeochromocytoma.
A test for sarcoidosis.

steps.x: E: Serum adrenal autoantibodies. Cause of Addison's: autoantibodies first.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has primary adrenal insufficiency on a short Synacthen test. Adrenal autoantibodies are negative. He is a smoker of 40 pack-years and has lost 9 kg in 4 months.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: When autoantibodies are negative, adrenal imaging looks for infiltration, infection, metastases or haemorrhage.

steps.x: Not autoimmune, and he may have cancer.

elim: The insufficiency is already primary; he needs a cause.
The diagnosis is already confirmed.
Already done.
Look for thyroid autoimmunity, not the adrenal cause.

steps.x: A: CT of the adrenal glands. Antibody-negative Addison's: image the adrenals.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has newly diagnosed Addison's disease and starts glucocorticoid replacement. The endocrine nurse explains how her hydrocortisone should be split through the day.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate regimen?
o: 10 mg on waking, 5 mg at midday, 5 mg mid-afternoon
5 mg on waking, 5 mg at midday, 10 mg at bedtime
questions.e: Hydrocortisone is given with most of the daily dose in the first half of the day, mimicking normal diurnal secretion.

clues: how her hydrocortisone should be split
steps.x: Copy the body: high in the morning, low at night.

elim: Gives cortisol at its normal low point.
A large evening dose is the opposite of the normal rhythm and disturbs sleep.
Does not mimic the morning peak.
Far too high a dose for replacement.

steps.x: A: 10 mg on waking, 5 mg at midday, 5 mg mid-afternoon. Hydrocortisone: biggest dose on waking.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man with Addison's disease takes hydrocortisone 10 mg, 5 mg and 5 mg daily. He still feels dizzy on standing and craves salt. His BP is 118/74 mmHg lying and 96/60 mmHg standing. His sodium is 131 mmol/L and potassium 5.5 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Fludrocortisone replaces aldosterone; persistent postural hypotension, salt craving, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia show mineralocorticoid deficiency.

steps.x: Glucocorticoid replaced, but mineralocorticoid deficiency persists.

elim: Blocks aldosterone and would worsen the hyperkalaemia.
He is salt-wasting; restriction would worsen it.
His potassium is already high.
Has no mineralocorticoid activity.

steps.x: C: Start fludrocortisone. Fludrocortisone replaces aldosterone.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman with Addison's disease takes hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. She has a runny nose and sore throat for 2 days. Her temperature is 37.1°C and she is eating and drinking normally with no vomiting. She asks whether she needs to change her tablets.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
questions.e: Sick day rules double the hydrocortisone dose during febrile illness above 37.5°C, keeping fludrocortisone the same; a mild afebrile cold needs no change.

steps.x: A minor afebrile illness without vomiting.

elim: Fludrocortisone stays the same; and she has no fever.
Fludrocortisone is never doubled on sick days.
Kept for vomiting or collapse.
Stopping steroids risks a crisis.

steps.x: A: Continue her usual doses. Sick day rules apply above 37.5°C.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has had Addison's disease for 3 years. He takes hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone and feels well. He attends his annual endocrine review and asks what checks are needed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate monitoring?
questions.e: Long-term Addison's care includes monitoring electrolytes and symptoms (with BP) to judge replacement.

steps.x: Routine review on stable replacement.

elim: Not needed in autoimmune disease.
The diagnosis is established and treatment suppresses nothing to test.
Cortisol levels are not used to titrate routine replacement.
Not needed unless he has diabetes.

steps.x: C: Electrolytes and symptom review. Monitor electrolytes and symptoms in Addison's.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman with Addison's disease is brought in with vomiting and abdominal pain. She has just been given hydrocortisone 100 mg IV. Her BP is 78/42 mmHg, pulse rate 124 bpm and capillary refill 4 seconds. Her potassium is 6.0 mmol/L and glucose 4.6 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: In adrenal crisis, give IV or IM hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately, then large-volume IV 0.9% saline if there are features of shock.

clues: just been given hydrocortisone 100 mg IV
steps.x: Steroid given, but she is still shocked.

elim: She is vomiting; high-dose hydrocortisone already has mineralocorticoid effect.
Contains potassium and she is hyperkalaemic; saline is used.
Does not resuscitate shock and worsens hyponatraemia.
Fluid resuscitation comes first.

steps.x: C: IV 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L fast. Adrenal crisis: hydrocortisone, then large-volume 0.9% saline.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man with known Addison's disease has had a chest infection for 3 days. His wife finds him collapsed and drowsy. The paramedics find a BP of 80/46 mmHg and pulse rate 118 bpm. He carries a steroid emergency card. There is no IV access yet.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: A known Addison's patient with intercurrent illness who collapses is treated as an adrenal crisis: immediate IV or IM hydrocortisone 100 mg.

steps.x: Collapse with intercurrent illness in Addison's, and no IV line.

elim: Treatment must never wait for tests in a suspected crisis.
There is no IV preparation; hydrocortisone is the life-saving drug.
He is drowsy and the dose is far too low.
A diagnostic test with no place in an emergency.

steps.x: B: IM hydrocortisone 100 mg. Adrenal crisis: give hydrocortisone 100 mg IM or IV immediately.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman is being discharged after a diagnosis of autoimmune Addison's disease. She is on hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. She lives alone and works as a flight attendant. The nurse prepares her for emergencies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate item to give her?
questions.e: Patients are given a hydrocortisone injection kit and taught to use IM hydrocortisone if vomiting, continuing until it stops.

steps.x: If she vomits, oral tablets will not work.

elim: Used for anaphylaxis.
Does not prevent a crisis.
Used for severe hypoglycaemia in insulin users.
Fludrocortisone is not doubled; hydrocortisone is the emergency drug.

steps.x: D: Hydrocortisone injection kit. Every Addison's patient needs a hydrocortisone injection kit.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with undiagnosed Addison's disease has emergency surgery for a perforated appendix. Despite 4 L of fluid and a noradrenaline infusion his BP stays at 72/40 mmHg. After IV hydrocortisone his BP rises within an hour.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his refractory hypotension?
o: Cortisol deficiency reducing vascular response to catecholamines
Loss of adrenaline from the adrenal medulla
questions.e: Cortisol maintains vascular tone and responsiveness to catecholamines; without it, physiological stress causes refractory hypotension and shock.

clues: After IV hydrocortisone his BP rises
steps.x: Pressors fail until cortisol is given.

elim: Aldosterone is deficient, and it retains rather than loses salt.
Causes water retention, not hypotension.
The cortex, not the medulla, is destroyed.
Would cause arrhythmia, and does not explain the response to hydrocortisone.

steps.x: A: Cortisol deficiency reducing vascular response to catecholamines. Cortisol is needed for vessels to respond to catecholamines.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman with Addison's disease has influenza with a temperature of 38.6°C. She has followed her sick day rules. Her daughter, a nursing student, asks why the hydrocortisone dose is increased when she is ill.
questions.q: Which best explains the sick day rules?
o: They correct hyperkalaemia caused by fever
They replace cortisol lost in sweat
They suppress the immune response to the virus
To mimic the normal cortisol surge during stress
questions.e: Healthy adrenals raise cortisol under stress; fixed replacement doses cannot, so sick day rules mimic this physiological surge.

clues: why the hydrocortisone dose is increased
steps.x: What does a normal adrenal do during illness?

elim: Fludrocortisone, not extra hydrocortisone, handles potassium, and its dose stays the same.
Steroids do not treat the infection.
Cortisol is not lost in sweat in meaningful amounts.
This is not the aim.

steps.x: E: To mimic the normal cortisol surge during stress. Sick day rules imitate the stress cortisol surge.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man has newly diagnosed Addison's disease. His sodium is 125 mmol/L, urea 10.2 mmol/L and BP 98/60 mmHg with a postural drop. His urine sodium is high despite his low blood sodium.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hyponatraemia?
o: Increased ADH from a lung tumour
Reduced sodium reabsorption in the distal nephron
questions.e: Aldosterone deficiency impairs renal sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the distal nephron, causing hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and volume depletion with hypotension.

steps.x: Salt is being lost through the kidney with volume depletion.

elim: Would cause a low urine sodium and no volume depletion.
SIADH causes euvolaemia and no hyperkalaemia.
Would give a low urine sodium.
Not a mechanism of hyponatraemia here.

steps.x: D: Reduced sodium reabsorption in the distal nephron. No aldosterone = renal sodium loss.

questions.stem: A 43 year old woman has autoimmune Addison's disease. Her friend has secondary adrenal insufficiency after pituitary surgery. Only the woman with Addison's disease has hyperkalaemia and needs fludrocortisone.
questions.q: Which best explains the difference?
o: The adrenal cortex is destroyed, so aldosterone is lost too
questions.e: In Addison's disease progressive destruction of the adrenal cortex reduces both cortisol and aldosterone; in secondary disease aldosterone is preserved because the renin-angiotensin system still drives it.

clues: Only the woman with Addison's disease has hyperkalaemia
steps.x: Primary disease loses the whole cortex; pituitary disease loses only ACTH drive.

elim: ACTH is a minor regulator of aldosterone.
The kidneys are normal.
Her friend also lacks cortisol but has normal potassium.
Aldosterone is made in the zona glomerulosa.

steps.x: D: The adrenal cortex is destroyed, so aldosterone is lost too. Primary = cortisol and aldosterone lost.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has primary adrenal insufficiency. His 9am cortisol is 60 nmol/L and his plasma ACTH is 480 ng/L (reference under 50). He has pigmented skin creases and gums.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason his ACTH is so high?
o: Excess melanocyte-stimulating hormone from the skin
Loss of cortisol negative feedback on the pituitary
Reduced ACTH breakdown by the liver
questions.e: Low cortisol removes negative feedback, so ACTH rises; ACTH comes from the same precursor (POMC) as MSH, causing pigmentation only in primary disease.

steps.x: Low cortisol with very high ACTH: the pituitary is responding normally.

elim: Would cause Cushing's disease with high cortisol.
Would cause very high cortisol.
MSH comes from POMC in the pituitary, not the skin.
Not a recognised mechanism.

steps.x: D: Loss of cortisol negative feedback on the pituitary. Primary failure removes feedback: ACTH (and MSH from POMC) rise.
